blocks.content: A proclamation imposing President’s Rule must be approved by both the Houses of Parliament within two months from the date of its issue.

rows: War, external aggression, or armed rebellion
Failure of constitutional machinery in state

items: President's Rule requires a simple majority in Parliament, whereas National Emergency under Article 352 requires a special majority.
In the landmark S.R. Bommai case (1994), the Supreme Court ruled that the proclamation of President's Rule is subject to judicial review.
The President revokes the proclamation on his own without requiring parliamentary approval.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: President's Rule can be proclaimed under Article 356 when the government of a state cannot be carried on in accordance with constitutional provisions.
Article 365 provides that failure by a state to comply with directions given by the Centre serves as a valid ground for imposing President's Rule.
Every proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within two months from its date of issue by a simple majority.
Once approved, President's Rule continues for six months and can be extended up to a maximum period of three years with parliamentary approval every six months.

The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 introduced constraints on extending President's Rule beyond one year unless a National Emergency is in operation or the Election Commission certifies holding assembly elections is difficult.
